PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.

workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions

than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's

tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

Comment class: other

**Step 1 done — PR‑1 merged as [#854](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/854) (`b30ef77`), approval №1 given.** Every Step‑1 row is checked; the endpoint map went in before the merge once the two routine URLs existed, so nothing is parked.

Two changes to the design landed inside PR‑1 and are worth naming here, because both simplify what Step 2 has to prove:

- **Invocation is a routine's API trigger**, verified against the routines docs rather than assumed. Firing a routine runs *its stored prompt*, and our `text` arrives wrapped as untrusted — so the payload names the item and the nonce and instructs nothing, and the session's instructions are a tracked file (`engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md`) that the routine's one-line prompt points at.
- **One call per item, never retried** (owner correction) — which deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather than simplifying it. There is no idempotency key on the endpoint, so a retry is precisely how two sessions land on one item. An unanswered call now leaves the item with the agent, and the janitor's agent leash settles it either way. `MAX_HANDOFF_ATTEMPTS`, the attempt counter and the bounded revert are all gone.

---

## Step 2 — the burst, in progress

- [x] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25)** — evidence: the dispatched tick ([run 31899008771](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31899008771)) created **12 standing items**, one per scheduled task, every one `task:blocked` + `origin:schedule` and stamped with its own next real anchor: [#860](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/860) `core/update` at 02:00Z (`daily-2h`), [#863](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/863) `growth-extract` at 03:00Z (`daily-1h`), the dailies at 04:00Z, the weeklies at Sunday 04:00Z. The two `manual` tasks were not instantiated, and the post-tick drain found nothing ready — adoption fired no work off-anchor, which is the whole property S25 asks for.

The issue list is now the dashboard the design describes: twelve open items, each stating its next wake.

Remaining rows in order, and what each still needs:

- **B2 roll + reason on record** — wake a task whose precondition declines; needs nothing.
- **B4 agentless path end to end** — next, via `basics/task-janitor`: prework-only, so it exercises wake → pick → claim → precondition → prework → `outcome:done` with no session involved.
- **B3 agentic happy path** — blocked on one manual step: the two routines need their one-line Instructions (`Read engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md and follow it.`) before a fire does anything sensible.
- **B5–B11** follow once B3 is live.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.

workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

work-item queue: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (#854)

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. **Primary Request and Intent:**

   The user's opening request was "Start work on 801" — GitHub issue [#801](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/801) in `missingbulb/Claudinite`, the phase plan for migrating task dispatch from the "slot" machinery to a **work-item queue** (`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md`). The issue specifies three steps with **two approval points**:
   - **Step 1 (PR-1, approval №1)**: the whole mechanism + canon flipped to `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"` in one PR — label vocabulary, tick workflow, executor workflow, janitor re-target, dependency fields + `after` yield + `create-work-item`, F8 signal exclusions, gate green.
   - **Step 2 (zero approvals)**: a same-afternoon validation burst driving real work through every live-only path (rows B1–B11), each row's acceptance being an issue URL showing a full lifecycle.
   - **Step 3 (PR-2, approval №2)**: fleet flip + slot machinery deletion.

   Subsequent explicit user requests, in order:
   - Drop the Status line from the design doc; answer whether a PR was open.
   - Wire the CCR invocation: the user asked whether they needed to set it up and what the secret names were.
   - **Simplify**: make the routine prompt a single line (`Read the instructions.md file and follow it.`), and remove the claiming/checking process because "The API should be called once per item."
   - Supply the two routine URLs after setting the secrets.
   - "lgtm 854 and continue" — merge PR #854 into main and carry on with the burst.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Work-item queue**: issues as the queue; a thin generator *tick* instantiates each recurring task's standing item at its anchor, readies blocked items, reclaims dead executor claims — pure label mechanics, no preconditions, no signals.
   - **The roll**: on a precondition no-go, a scheduled item is *not* closed — `Not-before` is stamped with the task's next anchor, it goes `task:ready → task:blocked`, and the reason is recorded on the item. This deletes the Actions run-ledger watermark.
   - **Standing-item model** (owner decision 13): the item carries "asked, declined, wakes at T"; the tick is a pure function of the clock and the issue list.
   - **Verified lease** (executor claim): swap label, post claim comment, re-read; earliest claim wins by **comment id** (not timestamp — GitHub's `created_at` has one-second granularity), **episode-scoped** (F18: claims before the last `EPISODE_MARKER` comment are dead, else the item livelocks).
   - **Occurrence guard, both halves (F13)**: an item `created_at >= anchor` OR `closed_at >= anchor` covers the occurrence.
   - **F16 self-heal**: duplicate standing items closed to the oldest, first.
   - **F15 post-claim re-verify**: pick filters are advisory; after winning a claim, re-verify against live state and revert if a conflicting item holds an earlier claim.
   - **`after` = pick-time yield, never a `Blocked-by` edge (S24)**: a rolling item never closes, so blocked-by would starve dependents of a quiet upstream forever.
   - **F17**: executor claim leash (60 min) must exceed every task's prework timeout, else prework is reclaimed while alive → livelock. Enforced at author time in `validateTaskDeclaration`.
   - **At-most-once invocation**: the routine `/fire` endpoint offers no idempotency key, so the executor calls **once per item and never retries**; this deleted the agent-side claim protocol entirely.
   - **Routine API trigger**: `POST [REDACTED:env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL]/v1/claude_code/routines/<trig_id>/fire`, `Authorization: Bearer`, `anthropic-beta: experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`, body `{"text": "<freeform, unparsed>"}`, response `{type, claude_code_session_id, claude_code_session_url}`. # Scheduled tasks — the per-project scheduling mechanism

How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs (per-project-scheduling design —
see issue #394). A repo
schedules **itself**, and the machinery is **three responsibilities, strictly
separated** (owner, 2026-08-06):

1. **The scheduler** — a vendored hourly Action
   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that evaluates each task's
   precondition in code, runs due tasks' prework, and **creates** dispatch
   issues (`ready-for-agent` `[claudinite-task]`) for agentic work. It creates
   task issues and nothing else about their afterlife.
2. **The executor** — a per-repo routine (fired by the label event) that
   executes **exactly the one task its triggering issue names**. It cares only
   about its task: no cleanups, no sweeping the queue, no merging of tasks, no
   updating other tracking issues.
3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about tasks that is *nobody's
   task*: escalating stale dispatches, reclaiming dead `agent-running` claims,
   re-arming lost trigger events, and printing a health review of the open
   dispatch set. Recovery runs once a day, in code, in one place — the stated
   trade is that a lost event now waits up to a day instead of an hour.
The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.

The checks below are the doctrine's enforcement; the phased rollout (and the
retirement of the legacy central planner it replaces) lives in the
per-project-scheduling migration record, linked from issue #394.

## What the checks guard

- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
  `workflow_dispatch` trigger, and a call into the vendored engine entry — no logic of its own
  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
  is the repo's **only** cron. Recurring work that had its own cron'd workflow
  becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted — its steps move into the
  task's worker. Don't keep it as a dispatch-only workflow for the task to fire:
  that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a workflow whose only
  caller is the thing that replaced it. (A workflow that must run *as an Action*
  for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, say — is the
  exception, and even then the task owns the schedule.) Off-band or multiple
  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
  safety, or manual runs.

- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
  default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency` (`hourly | daily-2h
  | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly | manual`), `precondition_signals` (the collector
  vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`), `expected_outcome` (`none |
  open-pr | merged-pr`), and a `precondition`. An agentic task (`agent_model !==
  none`) also carries `agent_instructions`, the worker file the agent reads; a
  `none` task runs no agent, so the field is not applicable and is omitted. The
  scheduler and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the dispatch
  issue — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
  static and runtime views can't drift. A task declares **no session scope** — see
  the next entry.

- **Session scope is retired; an executor's reach is how its repo is provisioned**
  (owner ruling, 2026-08-09). A dispatch rides the `ready-for-agent` label, and the
  executor session that fires on it carries whatever access that repo's routine was
  given — the sheepdog enforcer's spans the fleet because that repo *is* the fleet
  enforcer, not because any task asked. No task, and no pack, declares a scope.

  The task-level `session_scope` field is **deprecated, still honoured**: a lingering
  `'fleet'` routes to the `ready-for-agent-fleet` label, whose separate, broader
  executor routine exists only in the canon repo (its launcher prompt must end in the
  word `fleet`; the executor declines a dispatch that reaches the wrong routine). The
  canon home's curation tasks (`growth-promote`, `growth-discover-packs`) are the one
  standing use — the canon repo's ordinary executor does *not* hold the fleet, so the
  second label is what keeps that grant off it. Everything else drops the field. The
  deprecation is carried the standard way — an `@deprecated` tag on the contract
  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`), for linters and readers alike — and each
  sanctioned holdout pacifies the warning with a comment at its declaration site;
  there is no bespoke conformance check for it, deliberately.

- **Every run is bounded.** An agentic task (`agent_model !== none`) declares
  `agent_execution_timeout` — seconds bounding the agentic run
  (task-prework design §2, §6 — see issue #394).
  There is no platform wall-clock kill for a launched executor session, so the
  bound is best-effort: the executor surfaces it into the subagent's brief ("fail
  after N minutes") and the stale-`agent-running` backstop catches a dead session.
  Set it generously — extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling knob.

- **A task says which repo secrets it needs.** Preprocessing runs Action-side, so
  repo Actions secrets are reachable there and nowhere else in a task's life (an
  executor session carries none). A task lists what it needs in `required_secrets`;
  the wiring converge stamps each name into the scheduler workflow, so a worker
  reads it as ordinary environment, and baselining asks the owner (one standing
  issue) for any the repo hasn't configured. The adoption interview's posture, not
  a gate — nothing fails; the task that needs the secret just doesn't work yet. The
  consequence worth designing around: **a workflow that exists only to hold a
  secret is redundant** — fold its work into the task's preprocessing rather than
  dispatching and polling a second workflow from an agent.

Both guards are **relevance-first**: inert until their artifact exists, so
on a repo with neither artifact they are a no-op.

## The task folder

One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.mjs`** (the
self-contained declaration + `precondition(signals, config)`, the eligibility
gate as pure code) beside **`task.md`** (the worker spec the executing agent
follows), plus any deterministic helpers. The precondition both asserts
need-to-run and pre-decides scope: its `context` lines land verbatim in the
dispatch issue as binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate. `agent_model:
none` replaces the worker doc with an inline `.mjs` the scheduler runs directly —
no agent, no issue. This is the scheduled-task shape of the unattended-agents
routine-folder convention; the issue-driven-dispatch security rule (the issue is
data, the task path is code-validated, agent_model/expected_outcome come from the repo) lives
with that skill's agent practices.

### Three optional declarations, for a repo dispatching through the work-item queue

Additive, and inert under slot dispatch — declare one only when its rule applies.

- **`after: ['<pack>/<task>']`** — this task yields while a named upstream's item is live
  *this cycle*, and picks up the moment it converges or rolls. Declare it when your task
  reads what another task produces; never as a general priority hint. It is not a
  `Blocked-by` edge and must not be described as one.
- **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`** (default `requeue`) — declare `needs-human`
  only for a genuinely one-shot side effect (a store submission, an external notification):
  it makes every recovery path that would re-execute the task converge to triage instead.
- **`invocation_endpoint: '<name>'`** — a key into the repo's `taskScheduler.endpoints`, for a
  task whose agentic phase needs reach the repo's ordinary sessions lack. **Never a URL**: a
  task declaration is vendored verbatim into every consuming repo, so deployment detail and
  anything adjacent to a credential stay in that repo's own config.

A task's `prework_timeout` must stay under the executor's one-hour claim leash — a prework
that can outlive it is reclaimed while still running, and the item livelocks. The declaration
contract enforces this; do not raise a timeout past it, split the work instead.

## The precondition is the ONLY decision point

Task execution is **two similar, consecutive phases**: deterministic **prework**
(a subprocess the scheduler runs, Action-side) and **agentic work** (the
executor's subagent following task.md). Neither phase is "preparation" for the
other, and — the rule that matters — **neither may decide whether the task
runs**. That decision is the precondition's alone:

- A task that passes its precondition **runs**. The later phases must not find
  "new reasons to skip" — not timing, not repo state, not "already handled", not
  an open PR elsewhere. If a condition should stop the run, it belongs in the
  precondition, as code over signals, its verdict binding via the dispatch
  issue's Context.
- **Failures may stop a run** — a crash, a timeout, an API error converge to
  `needs-human`. Discretion may not.
- **"The work ran and produced nothing" is always legal** — that is an empty
  outcome, not a skip. The line: did the phase *do* the work and find it empty,
  or *decline* to do it?
- The conditional agent hand-off (a prework worker requesting the agentic phase
  via `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`) escalates on **work prework could not do** —
  never on a re-check of whether the run should have happened.

The `task-phase-discipline` world check (advisory, heuristic) hunts for tasks
that escape this — skip-language in task.md, cycle-skip strings in prework
workers.

## A precondition may claim the whole run

A verdict can carry **`exclusive: true`** beside `run: true` — *if I run this
cycle, I run alone*. Every other due task whose precondition said run is
**deferred**: no preprocessing, no dispatch issue, no inline work. It is there
because the hourly cron is not hourly (see the `github-actions-scheduling`
skill): a run that fires hours late finds several daily slots due at once, so the
hour of staging between the daily anchors collapses and a task anchored to run
*before* the others runs *beside* them. Baselining is the case it was built for —
it converges the mount, the wiring and the migration notes everything else then
executes against.

Claim sparingly, and **bound the claim at both ends**. A deferred slot is spent,
not queued: the run succeeds, the watermark moves past it, and that task runs
again at its *next* slot — tomorrow, or next week. So a claim on the routine case
quietly halves the fleet's throughput, and a claim with no upper bound (a
condition that stays true while something is broken) stops the repo doing
anything at all for as long as the breakage lasts. Baselining's shape is the
model: claim when the mount is more than a day stale, stop claiming past three
days, when it is a human's problem rather than a missed fire.

## The dispatch labels are a scheduler vocabulary

**Both ready labels are triggers**, so they belong on dispatch issues alone — never put
`ready-for-agent` or `ready-for-agent-fleet` on an ordinary issue, from a task or by hand.
Applying one starts an executor session that will find no valid dispatch and stop.
`agent-running` and `needs-human` carry no trigger and are the right vocabulary for a task
that needs to mark an issue as claimed or handed to a human; a task reusing them owns their
whole lifecycle on its own issues, since the scheduler's stale-claim backstop only converges
`[claudinite-task]` dispatch issues.

Nearly every dispatch rides `ready-for-agent`, and the session it starts carries the access that
repo's executor routine was provisioned with. `ready-for-agent-fleet` survives for the deprecated
task-level `session_scope: 'fleet'` — the canon's curation tasks, whose broader executor holds the
owner's repos so that grant stays off the canon's ordinary routine. Nothing new declares a scope.

## Dispatch lifecycle — every exit is terminal, and stale dispatches close

- Success → the executor comments the result and **closes** the issue.
- Failure → one comment naming what failed, `needs-human`. Nothing keeps
  updating a tracking issue about a failed state — one visible convergence,
  then it is a human's (or the janitor's) to look at.
- **Task gone** (the dispatch names a task the repo no longer carries — file
  removed, pack undeclared) → the executor **closes** the issue as not planned
  (resolve-dispatch's `task-gone` verdict). An obsolete dispatch is not an
  anomaly; it gets
  no `needs-human`.
- Every executor terminal state is recorded in code as a
  `claudinite-task-exec` line (`record-exec.mjs`, and resolve-dispatch for the
  code-decided verdicts) so the usage fold counts task statuses out of the
  captured conversation logs deterministically.

## A dormant project runs nothing

A project nobody is working on declares itself dormant in `.claudinite-checks.json`:

```json
"dormant": true
```

The scheduler stops before evaluating anything; the [fleet sweeps](../sheepdog/README.md)

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

# Task dispatch without slots — the work-item queue

The mechanism lives in [`engine/scheduler/queue/`](../../engine/scheduler/queue/),
behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`. A continuation of the owner's sketch (2026-08-12, reproduced in Appendix A), played against twenty timed
scenarios ([SCENARIOS.md](SCENARIOS.md)) and the field's prior art
([RESEARCH.md](RESEARCH.md)), with the owner's eight decisions of 2026-08-13
recorded in §15 and folded into the sections they changed. The phase plan
belongs to a tracking issue, not here. It supersedes
the slot machinery of
[per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3–§5](../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md) and
amends several of its §12 decisions (each amendment is named where it happens).
What it does **not** touch: the task folder anatomy (§1), the precondition
contract, prework and its secrets model
([task-prework DESIGN](../task-prework/DESIGN.md)), the outcome ceiling, the
security posture (the issue is data; behavior comes from tracked files), and the
usage-metrics records.

The shape in one paragraph: **work items are issues, available for work; any
number of executors pull from them.** A thin generator tick gives every
recurring task a standing work item at its anchor and flips blocked items
ready — pure label mechanics, no preconditions, no signals. An executor — a
GitHub Action by default, but anything that can read issues — picks up the
next ready item, claims it by label, evaluates the precondition (the only
place it ever runs): on a go it runs prework and hands off to agentic work (a
CCR session invoked by API); on a no-go the item **rolls** — stamped
not-before the task's next anchor, blocked, reason recorded — so the item
itself carries "asked, declined, wakes at T". Follow-ups, fan-outs, urgency,
and one-off forcing are all just *creating or waking work items*. There is no
slot id, no run-ledger watermark, no exclusive claim, and no label-event
re-arm.

---

## 1. What the slot machinery costs today

The current design is push-shaped: one hourly scheduler run decides, at a single
instant, everything that will happen — which tasks are due, whether they run,
what they may touch — and encodes the decision into dispatch issues that a
label-event-triggered session then executes. Every complication below is a
consequence of that shape.

- **The slot id is state smuggled into a title token.** `d2026-08-12`,
  `h2026-08-12T14Z`, `m2026-08` exist so that a scheduled occurrence has an
  identity — which the exactly-once guard needs (title search per slot), the
  stale backstop needs (the *leading character* of the slot id is parsed back
  into a period, `SLOT_PERIOD_MS`), and forcing needs (the `~f<runId>` marker
  appended so an operator re-run of an already-run slot isn't silently
  swallowed). Three mechanisms each decode a fragment of scheduler state out of
  a string in an issue title.

- **Due-ness lives in a platform side channel.** "Has this slot run?" is
  answered by the Actions run ledger of the scheduler workflow itself
  (`lastSuccessTime`) — a watermark that is not visible beside the work, must
  exclude forced runs to stay correct, and whose unreadability has to fail the
  whole run (an exit-0 abort would advance it past slots it never evaluated).
  The state the system actually cares about — *was this occurrence's work
  created?* — is derivable from the issues themselves, and nothing reads it
  from there. *(A first cut of the go/no-go ruling briefly reintroduced a
  ledger read; the standing-item model (§5) removed it again — the tick is
  now a pure function of the clock and the issue list.)*

- **A decision made at one instant cannot express ordering, only simultaneity.**
  The nightly chain's ordering is faked by anchor-hour staggering, which
  collapses whenever GitHub fires the cron late — hence the `exclusive: true`
  claim, a task-level hack whose cost is real: **a deferred slot is spent, not
  queued**, so a claim on the wrong night silently halves throughput. The
  system has no way to say "run B after A"; it can only say "run A alone".

- **Label-event invocation is lossy, and the loss shaped three mechanisms.**
  The executor routine fires only on a fresh `labeled` event; a lost delivery
  leaves an armed issue sitting forever. So: the janitor's re-arm
  (remove/re-add the label to emit a new event), the 20-minute grace window so
  a re-arm never hands a live session a rival, and the stale escalation that
  bounds the re-arm loop. The claim protocol then has to survive *duplicate*
  events (the read-swap-confirm lease). All of it is compensation for a trigger
  that neither confirms delivery nor can be polled.

- **Capacity, urgency, and follow-ups have no home.** There is exactly one
  implicit executor per repo and no way to add another; nothing distinguishes
  urgent work from routine work; a task cannot schedule a successor ("validate

{"number":801,"title":"Migration to the work-item queue: two PRs, one same-day validation burst","body":"The phase plan for [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md) (§14 points here). Design constraints from the owner (2026-08-13): **fewest disparate steps, fewest approval points, and certainty the same day** — we do not wait for a nightly run to learn whether the end state works. Deliberately generating real work (an engine release, pack updates, an extension release, research/extract material) to push traffic through every path is explicitly sanctioned.

**Approval points: two.** PR‑1 (mechanism + canon flip) and PR‑2 (fleet flip + slot deletion). Everything else is forcing and observing, which the mechanism itself defines as ordinary operations.

**What is already proven before step 1:** the simulator (`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`, in CI) rehearses every scenario in SCENARIOS.md, including the spec bugs it caught (F13, F14, the S28 stamped-wake precision). The coverage map in `sim/README.md` names exactly what only live traffic can prove — the burst below exists to cover precisely those rows.

Checkboxes track progress; each burst row's checkbox is checked only with an evidence URL (an issue showing the full lifecycle) appended beside it.

---

## Step 0 — rehearsal (done)

- [x] Simulator + scenario suite green in CI; coverage map names the live-only rows

## Step 1 — PR‑1 on canon: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (approval №1)

One PR containing everything, because the safety is the config flag and the disjoint issue families (`[claudinite-task]` vs `[claudinite-work]`), not PR granularity — rollback at any moment before Step 3 is a one-line config edit back to `"slots"`, with each mechanism's open items invisible to the other (proven: S29).

- [ ] Label vocabulary (`task:*`, `origin:schedule`, `outcome:*`) — create-if-missing wiring
- [ ] Tick workflow: cron at the hashed minute **plus `workflow_dispatch`** (the never-wait-for-the-cron lever the burst depends on)
- [ ] Executor workflow: post-tick drain + `labeled`-event runs, `required_secrets` and endpoint tokens stamped into its env (DESIGN §14 secrets path)
- [ ] Janitor re-target: executing-leash on the tick, agent leash, stale-ready, stuck-dependency sweep (F14)
- [ ] Dependency fields, the `after` pick-time yield, `create-work-item` + the wake/re-queue lever
- [ ] F8: signal collectors' self-trigger exclusions learn the new vocabulary **in this PR**, before any repo flips
- [ ] `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"` **on canon, in this same PR**; slot machinery stays in the tree, dormant on canon, live everywhere else
- [ ] Gate green: full suite (sim included) + conformance sweep
- [ ] **Approval №1: PR‑1 merged**

## Step 2 — the validation burst (same afternoon, zero approvals)

Fire the tick by `workflow_dispatch`, then drive **real work** through every live-only path. Each row's acceptance is an issue URL showing the full lifecycle on one item. Any row red = fix on canon (flag still reversible) and re-run that row — the burst is idempotent because forcing is idempotent.

- [ ] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25):** dispatched tick creates every task's item `task:blocked` wearing its next anchor — the issue list is the dashboard
- [ ] **B2 the roll + reasons on record (S1′):** wake a task with no work (`tidy-issues` on a quiet morning): one ask, roll to tomorrow, reason visible
- [ ] **B3 agentic happy path + real CCR invocation + records (S2):** touch a stale issue, wake `tidy-issues`: claim comment → prework → hand-off → live session → `outcome:done` + exec record
- [ ] **B4 agentless path + `required_secrets` end to end (§14 secrets 1–4):** bump the extension version so `store-release` has a genuine release to ship; prework consumes the store token from the stamped env
- [ ] **B5 the chain + yield (S4/S23):** cut an engine release (real baselining work) and stage extract material; wake `baselining`, watch `growth-extract` yield then run the same hour
- [ ] **B6 hourly cadence (S22):** file a real extractor request, watch `create-extractor` catch it within the hour; otherwise its hourly roll is the evidence
- [ ] **B7 missing-secret posture + re-queue (§14 step 7, F7, S19):** point a scratch task at an endpoint whose secret is deliberately unset: hand-off converges `needs-human` naming it; set the secret, re-queue, watch it converge
- [ ] **B8 force-while-executing mutex (S15):** while B3's agent runs, `create-work-item` its twin: it waits, then gets its own verdict
- [ ] **B9 multi-executor lease (S7):** B3–B6 running together give drain + label-event executor overlap; every item shows exactly one winning claim, no double execution
- [ ] **B10 follow-up fields (S17):** B4's release creates a real validate-in-2-days follow-up (`Blocked-by` + `Not-before`); creation and blocked readiness checked today, its wake is the one deliberately deferred check
- [ ] **B11 janitor leashes:** fire the janitor by dispatch after B2–B9; zero false escalations on rolling/blocked items (the S21 property, live)

## Step 3 — PR‑2: fleet flip + slot machinery deletion (approval №2)

- [ ] Engine release carrying the migration note: flip `dispatch` to `"queue"`; nothing to relabel (disjoint families — old open dispatch issues are drained by a human or closed obsolete, finite and visible)
- [ ] **Slot machinery deleted in this same PR** (slots.mjs, run-ledger math, exclusive claim, re-arm, `FORCE_TASKS` path, slot-conformance checks) — the no-lingering-legacy discipline
- [ ] **Approval №2: PR‑2 merged + engine release cut**
- [ ] Every member's baselining forced (the old mechanism's last act converges the new wiring) — no waiting for nightlies
- [ ] Per-member mini-burst (B1–B3 via each repo's dispatched tick) green for every member
- [ ] The migration reports itself through the mechanism it ships: per-member "flipped and burst-verified" fan-out items + a fan-in status item `Blocked-by` all of them (S18 live) — fan-in closed `outcome:done`

Rollback after PR‑2 is `git revert` of PR‑2 (the flag alone no longer suffices once slot code is deleted) — accepted, because Step 2 already proved the end state on canon before any member moved.

## Done means

- [ ] All Step‑2 rows have evidence URLs on this issue

**Approval points: two.** PR‑1 (mechanism + canon flip) and PR‑2 (fleet flip + slot deletion). Everything else is forcing and observing, which the mechanism itself defines as ordinary operations.

**What is already proven before step 1:** the simulator (`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`, in CI) rehearses every scenario in SCENARIOS.md, including the spec bugs it caught (F13, F14, the S28 stamped-wake precision). The coverage map in `sim/README.md` names exactly what only live traffic can prove — the burst below exists to cover precisely those rows.

Checkboxes track progress; each burst row's checkbox is checked only with an evidence URL (an issue showing the full lifecycle) appended beside it.

---

## Step 0 — rehearsal (done)

- [x] Simulator + scenario suite green in CI; coverage map names the live-only rows

## Step 1 — PR‑1 on canon: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (approval №1)

One PR containing everything, because the safety is the config flag and the disjoint issue families (`[claudinite-task]` vs `[claudinite-work]`), not PR granularity — rollback at any moment before Step 3 is a one-line config edit back to `"slots"`, with each mechanism's open items invisible to the other (proven: S29).

- [ ] Label vocabulary (`task:*`, `origin:schedule`, `outcome:*`) — create-if-missing wiring
- [ ] Tick workflow: cron at the hashed minute **plus `workflow_dispatch`** (the never-wait-for-the-cron lever the burst depends on)
- [ ] Executor workflow: post-tick drain + `labeled`-event runs, `required_secrets` and endpoint tokens stamped into its env (DESIGN §14 secrets path)
- [ ] Janitor re-target: executing-leash on the tick, agent leash, stale-ready, stuck-dependency sweep (F14)
- [ ] Dependency fields, the `after` pick-time yield, `create-work-item` + the wake/re-queue lever
- [ ] F8: signal collectors' self-trigger exclusions learn the new vocabulary **in this PR**, before any repo flips
- [ ] `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"` **on canon, in this same PR**; slot machinery stays in the tree, dormant on canon, live everywhere else
- [ ] Gate green: full suite (sim included) + conformance sweep
- [ ] **Approval №1: PR‑1 merged**

## Step 2 — the validation burst (same afternoon, zero approvals)

Fire the tick by `workflow_dispatch`, then drive **real work** through every live-only path. Each row's acceptance is an issue URL showing the full lifecycle on one item. Any row red = fix on canon (flag still reversible) and re-run that row — the burst is idempotent because forcing is idempotent.

- [ ] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25):** dispatched tick creates every task's item `task:blocked` wearing its next anchor — the issue list is the dashboard
- [ ] **B2 the roll + reasons on record (S1′):** wake a task with no work (`tidy-issues` on a quiet morning): one ask, roll to tomorrow, reason visible
- [ ] **B3 agentic happy path + real CCR invocation + records (S2):** touch a stale issue, wake `tidy-issues`: claim comment → prework → hand-off → live session → `outcome:done` + exec record
- [ ] **B4 agentless path + `required_secrets` end to end (§14 secrets 1–4):** bump the extension version so `store-release` has a genuine release to ship; prework consumes the store token from the stamped env
- [ ] **B5 the chain + yield (S4/S23):** cut an engine release (real baselining work) and stage extract material; wake `baselining`, watch `growth-extract` yield then run the same hour
- [ ] **B6 hourly cadence (S22):** file a real extractor request, watch `create-extractor` catch it within the hour; otherwise its hourly roll is the evidence
- [ ] **B7 missing-secret posture + re-queue (§14 step 7, F7, S19):** point a scratch task at an endpoint whose secret is deliberately unset: hand-off converges `needs-human` naming it; set the secret, re-queue, watch it converge
- [ ] **B8 force-while-executing mutex (S15):** while B3's agent runs, `create-work-item` its twin: it waits, then gets its own verdict
- [ ] **B9 multi-executor lease (S7):** B3–B6 running together give drain + label-event executor overlap; every item shows exactly one winning claim, no double execution

- [ ] **B11 janitor leashes:** fire the janitor by dispatch after B2–B9; zero false escalations on rolling/blocked items (the S21 property, live)

- [ ] Engine release carrying the migration note: flip `dispatch` to `"queue"`; nothing to relabel (disjoint families — old open dispatch issues are drained by a human or closed obsolete, finite and visible)
- [ ] **Slot machinery deleted in this same PR** (slots.mjs, run-ledger math, exclusive claim, re-arm, `FORCE_TASKS` path, slot-conformance checks) — the no-lingering-legacy discipline

content.content:
# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue, triggered by a `task:ready` / `task:urgent` label event for
# latency and by hand for a drain. It carries NO cron: the tick's own drain job is
# the poll that makes a lost label event irrelevant, so events here are latency
# sugar and never the only delivery.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the tick and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Prework is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing leash (60m): a hung runner has to be
    # killed by the platform before its claim is reaped and the item re-picked, or
    # a zombie's prework runs beside its replacement's (F17).
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # Hand-maintained, like the tick beside it: the canon runs its own engine
          # at the repo root and no converge writes its workflows, so this list is
          # what the stub's `# claudinite:secrets` stamp produces on a member.
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs
===== SCHEDULER =====
# Claudinite work-item queue — the generator tick and its drain (tasks-dispatch
# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER. The tick is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain is an ordinary executor run: it picks up what the tick just created, which
# is what keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event
# delivered. Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency
# sugar, which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron
# lever every forced run, migration and validation burst depends on.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '44 * * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:

# One tick at a time, always. The tick's duplicate-standing-item self-heal is
# written assuming exactly this — it closes every open family item but the oldest,
# which is safe precisely because two ticks never run at once.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-tick
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write        # read the repo + vendored engine; a task's prework pushes its delivery branch
  issues: write          # create / label / comment / close work items — the queue itself
  pull-requests: write   # a task's prework opens its PR and arms auto-merge
  actions: write         # dispatch a workflow a task drives (creating a workflow_dispatch event needs write; `read` silently 403s the POST)

jobs:
  tick:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Instantiate, ready and reclaim work items
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/tick.mjs

  # The post-tick drain. `timeout-minutes` MUST stay ≤ the engine's executing
  # leash (60m): a hung runner has to be killed by the platform before its claim
  # is reaped and the item re-picked, or a zombie's prework runs beside its
  # replacement's.
  drain:
    needs: tick
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 50
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Drain the queue
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # On a member this block is stamped by the wiring converge (the
          # `# claudinite:secrets` marker in the stub); the canon has no converge,
          # so its own list is written here, by hand, in the same commit.
          FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
          CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_FLEET_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A scheduled run reaches no one when it goes red, so escalate a whole-run
  # failure to a human-visible `workflow-failure` issue. Converges to ONE open
  # issue by a fixed title (create-or-comment), and ensures the label first since a
  # first-run failure may precede any label-ensure.
  report-failure:
    needs: [tick, drain]
    if: failure()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite scheduler run failed';
            await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' }).catch(() => {});
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${owner}/${repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            const body = `The Claudinite tick/drain run failed: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels: ['workflow-failure'], body });

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.

workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

work-item queue: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (#854)

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

work-item queue: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (#854)

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

PR-1 of the tasks-dispatch migration. Work items are issues; a thin tick gives
every recurring task a standing item at its anchor and flips blocked items ready,
and any number of executors pull from the queue — evaluating the precondition
exactly once, at pickup, and rolling the item to its next anchor on a no-go so
"asked, declined, wakes at T" lives on the item rather than in a run-ledger
watermark nobody can see.

The mechanism ships behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`, which only this repo sets to
"queue"; every member keeps the slot machinery until the fleet flip deletes it.
The two are disjoint by construction — separate issue families, separate
workflows, separate janitor sweep — so the rollback is the same config edit
backwards.

Invocation is a routine's API trigger, called ONCE per item and never retried:
the endpoint offers no idempotency key, so a retry is what would put two sessions
on one item. That single decision deleted the agent-side claim protocol rather
than simplifying it, and left an unanswered call to be settled by the janitor's
agent leash — a rule that already existed. The session's instructions are a
tracked file the routine's one-line prompt points at.

The phase plan for [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md) (§14 points here). Design constraints from the owner (2026-08-13): **fewest disparate steps, fewest approval points, and certainty the same day** — we do not wait for a nightly run to learn whether the end state works. Deliberately generating real work (an engine release, pack updates, an extension release, research/extract material) to push traffic through every path is explicitly sanctioned.

**Approval points: two.** PR‑1 (mechanism + canon flip) and PR‑2 (fleet flip + slot deletion). Everything else is forcing and observing, which the mechanism itself defines as ordinary operations.

**What is already proven before step 1:** the simulator (`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`, in CI) rehearses every scenario in SCENARIOS.md, including the spec bugs it caught (F13, F14, the S28 stamped-wake precision). The coverage map in `sim/README.md` names exactly what only live traffic can prove — the burst below exists to cover precisely those rows.

Checkboxes track progress; each burst row's checkbox is checked only with an evidence URL (an issue showing the full lifecycle) appended beside it.

---

## Step 0 — rehearsal (done)

- [x] Simulator + scenario suite green in CI; coverage map names the live-only rows

## Step 1 — PR‑1 on canon: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (approval №1)

One PR containing everything, because the safety is the config flag and the disjoint issue families (`[claudinite-task]` vs `[claudinite-work]`), not PR granularity — rollback at any moment before Step 3 is a one-line config edit back to `"slots"`, with each mechanism's open items invisible to the other (proven: S29).

- [x] Label vocabulary (`task:*`, `origin:schedule`, `outcome:*`) — create-if-missing wiring
- [x] Tick workflow: cron at the hashed minute **plus `workflow_dispatch`** (the never-wait-for-the-cron lever the burst depends on)
- [x] Executor workflow: post-tick drain + `labeled`-event runs, `required_secrets` and endpoint tokens stamped into its env (DESIGN §14 secrets path)
- [x] Janitor re-target: executing-leash on the tick, agent leash, stale-ready, stuck-dependency sweep (F14)
- [x] Dependency fields, the `after` pick-time yield, `create-work-item` + the wake/re-queue lever
- [x] F8: signal collectors' self-trigger exclusions learn the new vocabulary **in this PR**, before any repo flips
- [x] `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"` **on canon, in this same PR**; slot machinery stays in the tree, dormant on canon, live everywhere else
- [x] Gate green: full suite (sim included) + conformance sweep
- [x] **Approval №1: PR‑1 merged** — #854, `b30ef77`

## Step 2 — the validation burst (same afternoon, zero approvals)

Fire the tick by `workflow_dispatch`, then drive **real work** through every live-only path. Each row's acceptance is an issue URL showing the full lifecycle on one item. Any row red = fix on canon (flag still reversible) and re-run that row — the burst is idempotent because forcing is idempotent.

- [x] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25):** dispatched tick creates every task's item `task:blocked` wearing its next anchor — the issue list is the dashboard — [run 31899008771](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31899008771), 12 items #860–#870
- [x] **B2 the roll + reasons on record (S1′):** wake a task with no work: one ask, roll to tomorrow, reason visible — #860
- [ ] **B3 agentic happy path + real CCR invocation + records (S2):** touch a stale issue, wake `tidy-issues`: claim comment → prework → hand-off → live session → `outcome:done` + exec record
- [x] **B4 agentless path end to end:** #859 — wake → executor in 2s → claim → prework → `outcome:done`, closed in 26s, no session
- [ ] **B5 the chain + yield (S4/S23):** cut an engine release (real baselining work) and stage extract material; wake `baselining`, watch `growth-extract` yield then run the same hour
- [ ] **B6 hourly cadence (S22):** file a real extractor request, watch `create-extractor` catch it within the hour; otherwise its hourly roll is the evidence
- [ ] **B7 missing-secret posture + re-queue (§14 step 7, F7, S19):** point a scratch task at an endpoint whose secret is deliberately unset: hand-off converges `needs-human` naming it; set the secret, re-queue, watch it converge
- [x] **B8 force-while-executing mutex (S15):** #871 — queued behind the executing twin, then got its own verdict on release
- [x] **B9 multi-executor lease (S7):** #873 — three overlapping executors, exactly one claim, one execution
- [x] **B10 follow-up fields (S17):** #872 — `Blocked-by` + `Not-before` created and held blocked by the tick
- [x] **B11 janitor leashes:** [run 31900490000](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31900490000) — 12 blocked/rolling items, zero escalations
- [ ] All burst rows green

## Step 3 — PR‑2: fleet flip + slot machinery deletion (approval №2)

- [ ] Engine release carrying the migration note: flip `dispatch` to `"queue"`; nothing to relabel (disjoint families — old open dispatch issues are drained by a human or closed obsolete, finite and visible)
- [ ] **Slot machinery deleted in this same PR** (slots.mjs, run-ledger math, exclusive claim, re-arm, `FORCE_TASKS` path, slot-conformance checks) — the no-lingering-legacy discipline
- [ ] The pack update flow stages only `pendingSchedulerWorkflow`, so `claudinite-executor.yml` reaches no member — add it to the staged set in this PR's engine release
- [ ] **Approval №2: PR‑2 merged + engine release cut**
- [ ] Every member's baselining forced (the old mechanism's last act converges the new wiring) — no waiting for nightlies
- [ ] Per-member mini-burst (B1–B3 via each repo's dispatched tick) green for every member
- [ ] The migration reports itself through the mechanism it ships: per-member "flipped and burst-verified" fan-out items + a fan-in status item `Blocked-by` all of them (S18 live) — fan-in closed `outcome:done`

Rollback after PR‑2 is `git revert` of PR‑2 (the flag alone no longer suffices once slot code is deleted) — accepted, because Step 2 already proved the end state on canon before any member moved.

## Done means

- [ ] All Step‑2 rows have evidence URLs on this issue
- [ ] All members flipped; fan-in item closed `outcome:done`
- [ ] Slot machinery gone from the tree
- [ ] 48h of ordinary operation as *confirmation* — explicitly not the proof; the burst was the proof

input.head: claude/work-on-801-zm89p7
input.body:
Closes the Step 3 prerequisite recorded on #801: the pack update flow stages only `pendingSchedulerWorkflow`, so `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` reaches no member. Landing it now rather than inside PR‑2 keeps the fleet flip to one concern.

## The failure this removes

The tick and the executor are **one mechanism split across two files**. The tick creates standing items and readies what is due — it evaluates no precondition and executes nothing. So a member that received the tick without the executor has a generator with no worker: a queue that fills every hour and is never drained.

The reason that is worth a PR of its own is what it *looks like*. There is no error, no failed run and no red workflow — every tick succeeds, and the issue list fills with `task:blocked` items that quietly never move. From outside it is indistinguishable from a repo whose tasks all legitimately declined, which is the same shape as the silent-wiring-freeze class #797 exists to end.

## Shape of the change

`pendingExecutorWorkflow` is **additive** rather than a widening of the scheduler lane, because the two answer different questions:

| | scheduler lane | executor lane |
|---|---|---|
| who owes a file | every member | only `dispatch: "queue"` members |
| `pending: null` means | already converged | already converged **or** nothing owed at all |

That second column is why they could not share a function: for most of the fleet the honest answer is *"you owe no executor file"*, and folding it into a lane whose null means "converged" would make the two indistinguishable. The same distinction the scheduler lane had to learn in #797 is preserved on the other axis too — an unreadable stub reports an error rather than collapsing into "already converged".

Both lanes' errors now join onto `detail`, for the reason that lane already documents: a new result field only reaches a member once its worker catches up a cycle later, while `detail` reaches every fielded worker today.

## Verification

- New test asserts the pair is staged **in the same cycle** through the same withhold lane, that a slot member is owed nothing and that owing nothing is not an error, and that a blind stub read reports. Watched it fail against `main` first (`pendingExecutorWorkflow` undefined), then pass.
- Full suite from `git ls-files '*.test.mjs'`: **1765 pass, 0 fail**.
- Conformance sweep: **0 blocking, 58 advisory** against `main`'s 56. The two new ones are `file-placement` on the dynamic imports inside the new function — the identical class the neighbouring `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` already carries for the identical imports, and #858 settled that this rule is advisory with no acceptance entries.

Not covered here: the delivery is exercised against member fixtures, not a live member — no member is on queue dispatch until the fleet flip, which is PR‑2's own step.

Refs #801

I made it a separate function rather than widening the scheduler lane, because the two nulls mean different things — every member owes a file at the scheduler path, while a slot-dispatch member owes *no* executor file at all. ---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.
